REDIRECT CHAIN CHECKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your redirect chain loop, run too long, or dead-end?

Paste the hops a URL's redirects actually took and check for a redirect loop that never terminates, a chain longer than the single hop search engines recommend, an HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade, a permanent site move that used a temporary status code instead of a permanent one, and a chain that dead-ends in an error or is still redirecting with nowhere further to go.

Nothing is uploaded. The hop list you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device — see "Why can't this page follow the chain itself?" below for what the CLI adds.

1. Check a redirect chain

Get this from your browser's DevTools Network panel (the Status and Name columns, in order), or by running curl -sI against each hop by hand.

2. Hops parsed

#StatusURL

Findings

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

The CLI walks the real chain over HTTP itself, one hop at a time — no cross-origin restriction, because it isn't a browser, and it only reads each response's headers, never the body:

node check.mjs https://example.com/old-page --json
node check.mjs https://example.com/old-page --max-hops 5
node check.mjs https://example.com/old-page --recommended-max-hops 2

Get check.mjs, fetch-chain.mjs, and engine.mjs from the repo — plain Node 18+, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the URL you give it and the Location header that URL's own server sends back — nothing goes through this site. Exit code 1 when a danger-severity finding is produced or the chain could not be completed.

What's checked

CheckWhat it flagsSeverity
Redirect loopA URL earlier in the chain is visited again later in itDanger
Chain too longMore hops than recommended (default: 1) before landingNotice
Protocol downgradeA hop redirects from HTTPS back to HTTPDanger
Temporary code for a permanent moveA scheme/www normalization redirect uses 302/303/307 instead of 301/308Notice
Chain ends in an errorThe final hop is a 4xx or 5xx responseDanger
Chain incompleteThe last hop given is itself still a redirect, with nowhere further to goDanger

More: why redirect chains matter, and the most common ways they break. See also: how this differs from httpstatus.io's free redirect checker, and what checking a chain by hand with curl or DevTools misses.

Common questions

Why is a redirect chain longer than one hop a problem?

Google's own Search Central documentation on redirects advises keeping a redirect chain as short as possible — ideally a single hop — because search engines may not follow a very long chain at all, and every extra hop adds a full network round-trip of latency for every visitor, not just the first crawl. A chain that grows over years of site migrations without ever being cleaned up is the most common way this happens.

Why does a temporary redirect matter for a permanent site move?

A 301 or 308 tells a search engine the move is permanent, so it should consolidate ranking signal onto the new URL and eventually stop checking the old one. A 302, 303, or 307 says the opposite: "this is temporary, keep the old URL as canonical and check back later." Using a temporary code for what is actually a permanent scheme or www change (the same page, just upgraded to HTTPS or normalized to a canonical host) is one of the most common redirect mistakes and slows down exactly the ranking consolidation the move was meant to achieve.

Why can't this page follow the redirect chain itself?

A browser tab's fetch() to a different origin, by default, follows the whole chain silently and hides every intermediate hop and status code — exactly the information this tool needs. Asking for redirect: "manual" instead makes the response opaque, so JavaScript cannot read the status or the Location header of even the first hop. Either way, a page running in your browser cannot reliably inspect a cross-origin redirect chain. The zero-dependency CLI has no such restriction because it isn't a browser tab — it makes one real HTTP request per hop and reads each response directly.

Is this a full technical-SEO audit?

No. It checks specific, mechanically verifiable properties of the redirect chain you provide or the CLI fetches — loop detection, chain length, protocol downgrades, temporary-vs-permanent status codes, and the final destination's own status. It is not a crawl of your whole site and not a ranking guarantee.

It reports whether the redirect chain you provided satisfies specific, mechanically checkable rules — nothing more. It is not a ranking guarantee and not a full technical-SEO audit. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything you paste runs in your browser and is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Planning a migration? Redirect Map Checker checks a whole old-to-new redirect map for loops, chains and 404 targets before anything is deployed. Also worth a pass over the same URL: Canonical Tag Checker checks which URL a page's own rel=canonical link names as authoritative. Security Headers Checker checks a page's response-header security posture. Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check checks whether a sitemap's own freshness dates hold up.

vs-checking-a-chain-by-hand.html.text:
← back to the checker

This checker vs. checking a redirect chain by hand

The usual way to look at a redirect chain is curl -sI -L against the URL, or opening DevTools' Network panel and reading the Status and Name columns row by row. Both show you the hops. Neither one tells you whether any of what you're looking at is actually wrong -- a loop, a chain that's grown too long, a downgrade back to HTTP, or a permanent move that used a temporary status code. That reading is still yours, by eye, on every URL, every time.

What each one is for

Checking by hand costs nothing and needs no tool beyond what's already on your machine or in your browser. curl -sI -L (or curl -sI run once per hop, without -L, to see each Location header) and DevTools' Network panel both surface the real chain. For a one-off look at a URL you already suspect is fine, that's often enough.

This checker takes the same kind of hop data -- pasted from DevTools, or fetched for you by the CLI -- and runs it against five named checks instead of leaving the reading to you: a redirect loop, a chain longer than recommended, an HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade, a temporary status code used for what looks like a permanent move, and a chain that dead-ends in an error. It states which pattern was found and why it matters, and the CLI exits non-zero so it can fail a build instead of waiting for someone to notice.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I just want to see the raw hops for one URL, right now.Either one. curl -sI -L or DevTools is the faster path for a single ad-hoc look.
Does this chain loop back on itself?This checker. A loop is easy to miss by eye once a chain runs past two or three hops.
Is this chain longer than the single hop search engines recommend?This checker. Neither curl nor DevTools flags "one hop too many" -- there's no visual cue for it in either tool's output.
Does any hop quietly drop from HTTPS back to HTTP?This checker names the exact hop. In a long DevTools list it's one row among many, easy to scroll past.
Did a same-path scheme/www move use 302/303/307 instead of 301/308?This checker. Telling a temporary code apart from a permanent one, and knowing that distinction matters for ranking-signal consolidation, is a judgment call by-hand checking leaves entirely to you.
I want this checked automatically on every build, with nothing sent to a third party.This checker's CLI -- node check.mjs <url> runs from your own machine and exits non-zero on a finding, wireable into any CI as an ordinary step.

Common questions

Isn't running curl -sI -L or checking DevTools by hand enough to see a redirect chain?

It shows you the hops, which is the raw material this tool also needs -- but curl -L follows the chain silently by default and prints only the final response unless you add -v or drop -L and re-run it once per hop, and DevTools' Network panel requires you to read the Status and Location value of every row yourself. Neither tool tells you whether any of what you're looking at is actually a problem; that reading is left to you, and it has to be redone by eye on every URL you check.

What does checking by hand miss that this tool catches automatically?

Five specific patterns this tool names explicitly: a redirect loop (an earlier URL in the chain reappears later in it -- easy to miss by eye once a chain is more than two or three hops), a chain longer than the recommended single hop, an HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade buried in the middle of an otherwise-fine chain, a same-path scheme or www normalization that used a temporary 302/303/307 instead of a permanent 301/308, and a chain that ends in a 4xx/5xx error or is still redirecting when the data runs out. Curl and DevTools both show you the status codes; neither one tells you which combination of them is wrong.

Why is manually eyeballing chain length or a loop error-prone?

A loop only shows up as a URL that was already visited reappearing later in the list -- trivial to spot in a three-hop chain, and easy to miss once you're scrolling through eight or ten DevTools rows across an old migration nobody has cleaned up. Chain length has the same problem in reverse: there is no visual cue in curl's or DevTools' output for "this is one hop more than recommended," so the judgment call is silent and easy to skip entirely.

Can I wire this into CI so nobody has to check by hand again?

Yes -- that's the difference a script has over a habit. node check.mjs <url> makes the same real HTTP requests curl would, from your own machine, and exits non-zero the moment a danger-severity finding is produced, a hop's request fails, or the chain runs out of hops while still redirecting. Add it as an ordinary step in your own CI and a new loop or downgrade fails the build instead of waiting for someone to notice it in a manual curl trace.

They are not SEO, legal, or marketing advice, and they do not replace testing your own migration's real behavior. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

This page names no specific product. "Checking a redirect chain by hand" describes curl and browser DevTools, tools every developer already has, not any company's product or service.

Nothing leaves your browser. The checker this page links to parses pasted text entirely client-side; the CLI's requests go straight from your machine to the URL and Location headers it names. Nothing is proxied through this site.

vs-httpstatus-io.html.text:
← Redirect Chain Checker

Redirect Chain Checker vs. httpstatus.io

httpstatus.io is a well-known free web tool for inspecting a single URL: enter it into their site, and it follows the redirect chain from their own servers, showing you each hop's status code and response headers, along with checks like DNS resolution and SSL certificate details. For a quick, ad-hoc look at what a URL does, it is a solid, established first stop.

Redirect Chain Checker does a narrower and more specific job: it does not just show you the chain, it classifies it against five named misconfiguration patterns — a redirect loop, a chain longer than the single hop search engines recommend, an HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade, a temporary status code used for what looks like a permanent site move, and a dead-end error — and states in plain English why each one matters. Its zero-dependency CLI also runs the real requests from your own machine, never a hosted third-party service, so nothing about the URL you're checking is sent anywhere else.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I just want to see the raw chain, headers, DNS, and SSL info for one URL, quickly. httpstatus.io — that broad inspection is its job.
I want to know whether this chain has a loop, is too long, downgrades to HTTP, or used the wrong status code for a permanent move. Redirect Chain Checker — this tool names the pattern instead of leaving you to read the raw headers.
I want this checked automatically on every build, before it ships, with nothing sent to a third party. Redirect Chain Checker's CLI — node check.mjs <url> runs from your own machine and exits non-zero on a finding, wireable into any CI as an ordinary step.
I'd rather not paste a URL into a third-party site at all. Redirect Chain Checker's browser page works entirely from hops you paste in yourself (from your own DevTools Network panel), never sending the URL anywhere.

Neither tool replaces the other. httpstatus.io is a fine first look at a chain you don't yet understand. Once you know the chain exists, this tool answers the question a raw inspector doesn't: does it actually do anything wrong, by name, and will it stay that way in CI?

Common questions

Should I use Redirect Chain Checker or httpstatus.io?

Different jobs, and many people use both. httpstatus.io, based on its own public description, is a hosted web tool: you enter a URL into its site, it follows the redirect chain from its own servers and shows you each hop's status and headers, plus checks like DNS and SSL. Redirect Chain Checker instead classifies the chain against named misconfiguration patterns — a redirect loop, a chain longer than recommended, an HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade, a temporary status code used for what looks like a permanent move, and a dead-end error — and its zero-dependency CLI runs the real HTTP requests from your own machine rather than a third party's server.

Does httpstatus.io classify misconfiguration patterns the way this tool does?

Based on its own public description, httpstatus.io shows you the raw chain, each hop's status code, and response headers — it is a viewer/inspector, and reading the significance of what it shows (is this chain too long, does this hop downgrade to HTTP, is 302 the wrong code here) is left to you. This tool automates that reading: it names each pattern explicitly, states why it matters, and exits non-zero in CI when one is found.

Does the CLI send my URL anywhere?

No. The CLI makes its own HTTP requests directly from your machine to the URL you give it and to the Location header your own server sends back — nothing is proxied through this site or any other third party. httpstatus.io, by contrast, needs to send your URL to its own hosted service to follow the chain from there, which is the normal and necessary shape for a browser-only tool with no CLI.

Is this page affiliated with httpstatus.io?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by httpstatus.io. httpstatus.io is named here only to describe what that tool does and how it differs from this one, based on its own public description.

More: why redirect chains matter.

why-redirect-chains-matter.html.text:
← Redirect Chain Checker

Why redirect chains matter

A redirect chain is what happens between the URL someone typed, clicked, or a search engine indexed, and the page that finally loads. When that path is one hop — a single 301 straight to the current URL — it is invisible and free. Every hop past the first one is a cost somebody is paying without necessarily knowing it.

How a chain grows without anyone deciding it should

Nobody sits down and designs a four-hop redirect chain. It accumulates one migration at a time: a site moves from http to https, then a year later from www to the bare domain, then a URL structure change moves an old path to a new one — each change reasonable on its own, and each old redirect left pointing at the previous target instead of updated to point straight at the current one. The fix each time is simple — point every existing redirect at the final destination, not the last one — but it requires remembering every old redirect exists, which is exactly what nobody does three migrations later.

The two costs of a long chain

Latency, first: each hop is a full network round trip before the browser even starts loading the real page, and that tax applies to every visitor who follows an old link or bookmark, not just a one-time crawl. Crawl behavior, second: Google's own Search Central documentation on redirects advises keeping a chain as short as possible — ideally a single hop — because search engines may not follow a very long one at all the way a browser will. A page several hops deep in an old migration can simply stop being indexed under its current URL, with nothing in your analytics obviously pointing at "the redirect chain" as the cause.

Why a redirect loop happens at all

The most common cause is two independent redirect rules that each assume the other has already run — an HTTPS-enforcement rule and a www-normalization rule configured in the wrong order, or split across two systems (a CDN in front of an origin server) that each redirect the exact case the other one just produced. It is easy to miss in ordinary browsing: a browser that has cached an earlier successful load, or that gives up and shows its own "too many redirects" error after an internal limit, may never show you the loop the way a fresh crawler or a strict HTTP client hits it immediately.

301 vs. 302, and why the difference is not cosmetic

A 301 (or 308, which additionally preserves the original request method) tells a search engine the move is permanent — consolidate ranking signal onto the new URL and stop treating the old one as canonical. A 302, 303, or 307 says the opposite: this is temporary, keep checking the old URL. Using a temporary code for what is actually a permanent scheme or host normalization — the single most common shape this produces — delays exactly the ranking consolidation the move was meant to achieve, sometimes for months.

Finding these mechanically rather than by inspection

All four of the above — chain length, protocol downgrade, wrong status code for a permanent move, and an outright loop — are mechanically checkable from the chain itself, with no judgment call. Redirect Chain Checker runs those checks: paste a hop list you captured from your browser's Network panel, or run the CLI to walk the real chain over HTTP and get the same report automatically, wireable into CI as a regression gate.

Common questions

How does a redirect chain usually grow this long by accident?

One site migration at a time. A site moves from http to https (hop 1), then from www to non-www a year later (hop 2), then a URL structure change moves /old-path to /new-path (hop 3) — each individually reasonable, and each one left in place rather than updated to point straight at the current URL. Nobody adds three hops on purpose; it accumulates because updating every old redirect target every time something moves again is easy to forget.

What is the actual cost of a long redirect chain, beyond "it looks messy"?

Two costs, and they are different. First, latency: every hop is a full network round trip before the browser even starts loading the real page, and that delay applies to every single visitor, not just a search engine crawling it once. Second, crawl behavior: Google's own Search Central documentation on redirects advises keeping a chain as short as possible because search engines may not follow a very long one at all — so pages several hops deep in an old migration may simply stop being indexed under their current URL.

Why does a redirect loop happen at all — wouldn't someone notice?

The most common cause is two independent redirect rules that each assume the other has already run — an HTTPS-enforcement rule and a www-normalization rule configured in the wrong order, or on two different systems (a CDN and the origin server) that each redirect the case the other one just produced. It is easy to miss because a person testing in a browser that has cached an earlier successful load, or that stops following redirects after its own internal limit, may never see the loop that a fresh crawler or a strict HTTP client hits immediately.

Is a 302 redirect ever the right choice for a permanent move?

No — if the move really is permanent, 301 (or 308, which preserves the request method) is the correct code by definition, and using 302 for it is the mistake this tool flags. A 302 is correct for something genuinely temporary: an A/B test, a maintenance page, a seasonal redirect that will be reverted. The distinction search engines actually act on is exactly the one in the status code's own name, and using the wrong one for a permanent change is what delays ranking signal moving to the new URL.
